Andras Szkharosi
an'drash sk-ha'ro-shee
n. (Andras Szkharosi Horvat, active 1542–1549, Hungarian Protestant preacher at Tallya and the sharpest verse satirist of the Hungarian Reformation)
Szkharosi, Hungarian, of Szkharos, now Sarkad; Horvat, Hungarian, a Croat; Andras, the Hungarian form of Andrew, from Greek aner, a man.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Andras Szkharosi Horvat was a friar who became a Protestant preacher at Tallya in the Hegyalja wine country, and who between 1542 and 1549 wrote a handful of long poems in Hungarian which are the fiercest things in the literature of the Hungarian Reformation. They are not hymns. They are indictments in verse, meant to be sung or recited to people who could not read, against the worship of images, the selling of masses, the pride of the clergy, the oppression of the peasant by the landlord, and the sins of the nation which, he said plainly, had brought the Turk upon it. He took the prophets as his model and did not soften the application: if Israel was carried away for idolatry and injustice, Hungary at Mohacs had been broken for the same causes, and the remedy was repentance and not a crusade. The poems were printed at Krakow in the collection of Gal Huszar's circle and were read for a century. Nothing is known of his death. The dictionary keeps him for his method. He is the clearest Hungarian case of the Reformation preached in the common tongue, in the common measure, to people who owned no book—and of national calamity read, in the prophets' manner, as the judgment of God upon a people's sin rather than as mere misfortune.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a satire as a discourse exposing vice or folly; a plague as any great natural evil or calamity; and to reprove as to blame, to chide to the face.

expand to see more

SATIRE, n. [L. satira.] A discourse or poem in which wickedness or folly is exposed with severity; keenness and severity of remark.

PLAGUE, n. [L. plaga, a stroke.] Any thing troublesome or vexatious; a pestilence; any great natural evil or calamity.

REPROVE, v.t. [L. reprobo.] To blame; to censure; to chide to the face; to charge with a fault.

IDOLATRY, n. [Gr. idol, and service.] The worship of idols, images, or any thing made by hands, or which is not God.

VERSE, n. [L. versus.] A line consisting of a certain succession of sounds and number of syllables; metrical language.

Key Scripture

Exo 20:4 — "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:"

Psa 115:4 — "Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands."

Jer 23:16 — "Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD."

Hab 2:18 — "What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols?"

Modern Corruption

Hungarian verse satirist who named image worship, clerical greed and the oppression of the peasant as the sins for which God had given the kingdom to the Turk.

expand to see more

The corruption he attacked was image worship, and the dictionary names it with him. “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) is the second commandment, and the medieval church had not abolished it so much as explained it away by distinguishing the honour paid to the image from the worship due to God—a distinction the common people never made and were not meant to make, since the images were credited with the cures. Szkharosi wrote for those people and used their own measure to tell them what the commandment said.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the prophetic reading of national disaster. Modern writing on Mohacs treats the catastrophe as a matter of artillery, alliances and Habsburg politics, and so it was; Szkharosi insisted that it was also the hand of God upon a people, which is what every prophet says about every such defeat. The dictionary holds both: secondary causes are real, and they are the instruments of a providence that is moral.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pesel (H6459), a carved image; Hebrew elil (H457), a worthless thing, an idol.

expand to see more

Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven or carved image; “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image”, Exodus 20:4.

Hebrew temunah (H8544) — a likeness, a form; “or any likeness of any thing”, Exodus 20:4.

Hebrew atsab (H6091) — an idol, a shaped thing; “Their idols are silver and gold”, Psalm 115:4.

Hebrew hebel (H1892) — vanity, emptiness, a breath; “they make you vain”, Jeremiah 23:16.

Hebrew massekah (H4541) — a molten image; “the molten image, and a teacher of lies”, Habakkuk 2:18.

Usage

"“Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) — the second commandment put into Hungarian verse for people who owned no book."

"“Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4) — preached at Tallya in the Hegyalja between 1542 and 1549."

"“they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD” (Jer 23:16) — against the clergy who sold masses."
